newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Massacre survivors make pilgrimage to Port Arthur.
newsitem.headline: Massacre survivors make pilgrimage to Port Arthur.

text.p: Survivors of the Port Arthur massacre made an emotional pilgrimage on Monday to the scene of the 35 killings, strolling among stone ruins which echoed a year ago to the crack of gunfire.

Wandering around the old Port Arthur penal colony, crunching across lawns carpeted with fallen leaves, they retraced the steps that on April 28 last year linked their lives forever with Australia's worst mass murder in modern times.

Unmolested by reporters assigned to cover the anniversary, the 100 or so survivors and family of the victims roamed the site of their real-life nightmare in quiet reflection after attending a public remembrance service at Port Arthur.
Some walked to the remains of the Broad Arrow Cafe, partly demolished out of respect for the dead, where they left flowers for the 20 people who died there at the height of the massacre.
By the end of the day bouquets covered much of the floor of the small cafe, placed where the victims fell.
"To my lovelies," read an anonymous card attached to a bunch of pink blooms left beside the cafe's entrance. "Twelve months have gone. Love's sweet memories of you still remain."
Other mourners stopped at three old eucalytpt trees just inside the main gateway to the Port Arthur site where a mother, Nanette Mikac, and her two infant daughters were killed.
Walter Mikac, who was playing golf when his family was shot dead, planted three small white wooden crosses beneath the trees where Nanette and daughters Madeline, 3, and Alannah, 6, fell.

Pinned to each tree is a wreath of yellow flowers. One of the cards reads: "To my darling Maddie, my heart still bleeds for your beautiful smile and curly locks. You are a part of me that can never be replaced. Your loving dad, Walter XXXX."
In time, all of the survivors and bereaved family made their way to the Port Arthur waterfront where they joined in prayer before a simple wooden cross bearing the names of all 35 victims.
The cross, too, stood over a pile of flowers.
The young man who killed all 35 people, Martin Bryant, was confined on Monday to a suicide-proof prison cell about an hour's drive away in the Tasmanian state capital, Hobart.
Bryant, 29, is serving life imprsonment without parole in Hobart's Risdon prison.
Described at his sentencing in November as a social misfit with the mental age of a child, Bryant probably needed reminding of Monday's anniversary, in the view of one psychiatrist.
"But I'm fairly certain people around the prison will have reminded him," Hobart psychiatrist Ian Sale, who has assessed Bryant's mental state, told reporters at Port Arthur.
